summary:
Neither gender identity nor gender expression is criminalised in Venezuela, and homosexuality is legal, with a universal age of consent of 16 and no differential age for same-sex conduct. Enforcement practice does not follow the statute: in May 2026 NGOs including the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state, in which around 30 people were detained, officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, detainees were extorted, and those held were accused of "committing the crime of homosexuality".

There is no working route to legal gender recognition. A 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Tribunal of Justice requires each case to be assessed individually, supported by certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal has not granted the requested name and gender changes. The identity-document agency SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people may request a new identity card matching their gender identity, but no administrative procedure or mechanism exists to enact the relevant article, so identity-card information cannot in practice be changed. A trans visitor therefore travels on documents that do not reflect their gender presentation, with the mismatch visible at immigration and hotel registration.

No law in Venezuela provides anti-discrimination protection on grounds of gender identity, and there is no hate-crime statute, so conduct targeting trans people carries no dedicated legal penalty. The statute book also sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions, and no legal framework governs access to gender-affirming care.

Hostility from the state has been directed at openly LGBT politicians. Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla, a Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian, a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody, as reported on 13 December 2015. Following the disputed July 2024 election, LGBTQ Venezuelans faced what the Washington Blade described on 10 September 2024 as unprecedented persecution tied to the political crisis; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 September 2024. Against that record, Tamara Adrián ran for the National Assembly in 2015 as Venezuela's first transgender candidate, and Adrián and Mantilla were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of the legislature.

International protection bodies treat the situation as documented and referenceable. The European Union Asylum Agency maintains a dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in Venezuela within its country-focus material covering the reference period through 2025, used in international protection decisions, and AFS and the Vance Center published an LGBTQ guide covering Venezuela in October 2024.

Family law offers partial recognition only. An equal-marriage bill was to be presented to the National Assembly in late January 2014, and no later enactment is recorded. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, while lesbian couples are allowed to access IVF. On 15 December 2016 the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ruled that a baby may be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames, based on Article 75 of the Constitution, and declared that the state must protect all families without distinction so that children and teenagers born into same-sex families enjoy the rights and guarantees of children born into opposite-sex families.
tangentialFactors:
Venezuela has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and in May 2016 the National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. The Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016, an official reversal that indicates how quickly symbolic protection in this area has been withdrawn. The government has recently begun participating in Pride events.

Public-opinion data is mixed and dated in different directions. A Cronica Uno poll of 2–3 March 2023 found a majority of Venezuelans agree that the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens, 82% knew the term LGBTIQ+ with 13% not knowing it, and 36% thought gay, lesbian or bisexual orientation is innate. An Equilibrium CenDE poll in 2023 found 48% of Venezuelans supported adoption by same-sex couples, 34% totally and 14% somewhat, against 39% opposed. A 2013 Pew survey recorded 57% of 18–29-year-olds saying homosexuality should be accepted by society, against 51% of 30–49-year-olds and 45% of those over 50.

Comparable Latin American jurisdictions have moved to statutory gender recognition and partnership rights, while Venezuela has left recognition in the hands of individual Supreme Tribunal of Justice proceedings with no granted outcome on record. The gap between formal legality and police practice seen in the Barquisimeto raid distinguishes Venezuela from jurisdictions where decriminalisation is accompanied by enforced non-discrimination.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source Venezuelan entry, visa or border-document rules, including whether immigration authorities accept identity documents whose gender marker differs from the holder's presentation, or how gender markers are read on foreign passports. That question is unresolved here and is not answered by the domestic SAIME procedure, which governs national identity cards only.

Whether the individuals detained in the May 2026 Barquisimeto raid were charged, and whether any proceedings followed the allegations of warrantless entry and extortion, is not recorded in the available material. The outcome of the 2017 Supreme Tribunal of Justice gender-recognition action beyond the stated non-granting of name and gender changes is likewise unresolved.

The status of the equal-marriage bill first reported in January 2014 is stated only as having no later enactment on record; no source in the inventory confirms its formal withdrawal or rejection. The legal basis on which police in Barquisimeto asserted a "crime of homosexuality" is not documented, and no hate-crime or gender-identity discrimination statute appears in the sourced material. The public-opinion figures cited are dated 2013, 2023 and do not measure attitudes specific to trans people.
